Memory Jogger.new: Private racially restrictive covenants do not themselves violate the Fourteenth Amendment, but a state court's enforcement of them is state action that denies equal protection; a unanimous six-Justice Court reversed Missouri and Michigan decrees ousting Black families from homes they had bought from willing sellers (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/334/1/}{Justia}).

Judicial Votes.new: The Supreme Court \textbf{reversed} the judgments of the Supreme Courts of Missouri and Michigan by a \textbf{6--0} vote. The cases were argued on January 15--16, 1948, and decided on May 3, 1948 (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/334/1/}{Justia}):

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Majority Opinion:} Chief Justice Vinson delivered the opinion of the Court, joined by Justices Black, Frankfurter, Douglas, Murphy, and Burton.
    \item \textbf{Concurring Opinions:} None.
    \item \textbf{Dissenting Opinions:} None.
    \item \textbf{Not Participating:} Justices Reed, Jackson, and Rutledge took no part in the consideration or decision of the cases.

Judicial Votes.src: Although the Justices issued no public explanation in the \textit{United States Reports}, historical scholarship and contemporary accounts attribute their recusals to their ownership of residential properties subject to racially restrictive covenants.

Analysis of Opinions.from: In the companion District of Columbia case

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Enforcement Barred): A Religious Covenant Used to Divest Title.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: A homeowners' association sues in state court to enforce a recorded neighborhood covenant barring sales to non-Christian buyers, seeking to divest title after a willing owner sells her home to a Muslim family.

Scenario~A falls squarely under \textit{Shelley} (and violates the Fair Housing Act): third parties are enlisting judicial coercion to override a voluntary transaction and enforce neighborhood-wide exclusion.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Enforcement Barred): Damages Against the Selling Owner.} A recorded subdivision covenant bars sale to persons of a particular national origin. An owner sells to a willing buyer of that origin, and the neighbors, rather than seeking to evict the buyer, sue the seller in state court for breach of the covenant and ask for money damages. Under \textit{Shelley}, a state court that lends its coercive power to a discriminatory private agreement is itself acting for the State, and \textit{Barrows v. Jackson}, 346 U.S. 249 (1953), applied that reasoning to damages actions because the threat of liability would pressure owners to refuse willing buyers. The court must deny relief; the Equal Protection Clause reaches national-origin classifications as well as race (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/334/1/}{Justia}).
\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (No Constitutional Violation): Excluding a Guest From One's Own Home.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: A private homeowner bars a neighbor from a home dinner party because of the neighbor's religion and calls police to prosecute the neighbor for criminal trespass.

Examples: Future Applications.new: Unlike in \textit{Shelley}, no willing owner is being overridden: the State's trespass law enforces the owner's own choice about her own home, and

Examples: Future Applications.src: an \textit{unwilling} owner's personal trespass exclusion reflects private associational autonomy rather than third-party coercion

Examples: Future Applications.new: . Reading \textit{Shelley} to reach this case would turn every invocation of neutral property law into constitutional state action.
\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (No State Action): Enforcing a Non-Disparagement Clause.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: A private contractor petitions a state court to enjoin a former employee from publishing a critical op-ed in breach of a voluntary settlement's non-disparagement clause. The employee cites \textit{Shelley}, claiming judicial enforcement triggers First Amendment strict scrutiny.

Although \textit{Shelley}'s broad language invites the argument, modern courts reject extending its attribution rationale to private speech contracts (\textit{United Egg Producers}), preserving private ordering under \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/587/17-1702/}{\textit{Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck}, 587 U.S. 802 (2019)}, while confining judicial state action to racial discrimination or core courtroom processes such as peremptory strikes (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/500/614/}{\textit{Edmonson v. Leesville Concrete Co.}, 500 U.S. 614 (1991)}).

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Fence-Sitter (Uncertain): A Testamentary Condition Based on a Beneficiary's Spouse.} A will leaves a large bequest to the testator's grandson on the condition that he marry a person of the testator's own faith within seven years; otherwise the money passes to a charity. The grandson marries outside the faith and asks the state probate court to strike the condition, arguing that judicial enforcement is state action under \textit{Shelley}. He can point out that the court's decree would give legal force to a private religious exclusion. But no willing seller and willing buyer are being overridden: the court would simply carry out the testator's own disposition of his own property under neutral probate rules, the posture that \textit{Evans v. Abney} treated as permissible. Because \textit{Shelley}'s reach beyond restrictive covenants has never been defined, the outcome is uncertain.
